crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
children.blurb: The AI enablement audit in an investment firm examines how artificial intelligence is introduced, approved, used, and monitored across the investment lifecycle.

children.name: Fair Lending and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Fair lending and bias testing is the practice of checking whether credit decisions, pricing, marketing, and servicing treat applicants and borrowers fairly regardless of protected characteristics such as race, ethnicity, sex, age, or national origin.

children.name: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
children.blurb: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the practice of translating how an AI system reaches its outputs into language and evidence that non-specialists can assess.

children.name: Protecting Material Non-Public Information
children.blurb: Protecting material non-public information covers the rules and practices that keep confidential, price-sensitive facts about a company or its securities from being used in trading.

children.name: Verifying What a Model Produced
children.blurb: Verifying what a model produced means checking the output of an AI system against the purpose it was meant to serve, the sources it relied on, and the rules that apply to its use.

sections.body: Governance and fiduciary risk covers the work of proving that an AI system used in finance behaves the way the law and the client relationship require. In practice this means auditing how models are deployed across a firm, testing lending decisions for disparate impact, writing explanations that a regulator or client can follow, keeping material non-public information out of model inputs and outputs, and checking what a model actually produced before anyone relies on it. These are operational jobs, not philosophical ones, and they are done by compliance staff, model risk officers, internal auditors and outside counsel. The field sits where machine learning meets the duties that already attach to anyone handling other people's money.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature. Fair lending testing has decades of statistical method behind it, and the basic mechanics of an enablement audit are well understood, even if firms run them unevenly. Other parts are genuinely unsettled. Explaining a large model to a regulator in a way that satisfies a disclosure obligation is still an open problem, and the tools for verifying model output are younger than the models they check. Data loss prevention has strong precedent from email and trading surveillance, but applying it to prompts and model context is new. The honest limit across all of it is that governance work produces evidence of process, not proof of correctness, and no audit removes the underlying uncertainty about what a model will do next.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the sequence a firm would actually work through. The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms is the entry point, covering how deployment is reviewed across a business before and after a system goes live. Fair Lending and Bias Testing narrows to credit decisions and the statistical tests that regulators expect to see. Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients takes the outputs of those tests and asks how they are communicated to people outside the firm. Protecting Material Non-Public Information handles the boundary problem, keeping confidential deal and trading data away from models and prompts. Verifying What a Model Produced closes the loop, covering the checks that happen after a model returns an answer and before a human acts on it. A reader new to the area should start with the audit page, while someone already in compliance will likely go straight to the explanation or verification pages.
